source_text: Quis nunc medullas Scripturarum magis nosset, quam ipsa Christi schola? quos et sibi discipulos Dominus adoptavit, omnia utique edocendos; et nobis magistros adornavit, omnia utique docturos. Cui potius figuram vocis suae declarasset, quam cui effigiem gloriae suae revelavit, Petro, Jacobo, Joanni, et postea Paulo, quem paradisi quoque compotem fecit ante martyrium? An et illi aliter quam sentiunt scribunt, fallaciae magistri, non veritatis? Petrus quidem ad Ponticos: Quanta enim, inquit, gloria, si non ut delinquentes puniamini, sustinetis! Haec enim gratia est, in hoc et vocati estis, quoniam et Christus passus est pro nobis, relinquens vobis exemplum semetipsum, ut assequamini vestigia ipsius. Et rursus: Dilecti, ne expavescatis ustionem, quae agitur in vobis in tentationem, quasi novum accidat vobis: etenim secundum quod communicatis passionibus Christi, gaudete, uti et in revelatione gloriae ejus gaudeatis exultantes. Si dedecoramini in nomine Christi, beati estis, quoniam gloria et Dei spiritus requiescit in vobis, dum ne quis vestrum patiatur, ut homicida, aut fur, aut maleficus, aut alieni speculator. Si autem ut christianus, ne erubescat; glorificet autem Dominum in nomine isto. Joannes vero, ut etiam pro fratribus nostris animas ponamus, hortatur, negans timorem esse in dilectione: Perfecta enim dilectio foras abjicit timorem: quoniam timor poenam habet; et qui timet, non est perfectus in dilectione. Quem timorem intelligi praestat, nisi negationis auctorem? Quam dilectionem perfectam affirmat, nisi fugatricem timoris, et animatricem confessionis? Quam poenam timore puniat, nisi quam negator relaturus est, cum corpore et anima occidendus in gehenna? Quod si pro fratribus, quanto magis pro Domino moriendum docet, satis de Apocalypsi quoque sua instructus haec suadere! Mandaverat etenim spiritus ad angelum ecclesiae Smyrnaeorum: Ecce diabolus ex numero tuo conjiciet in carcerem, ut tentemini diebus decem. Esto fidelis ad mortem usque, et dabo tibi vitae coronam. Item ad Pergamenorum de Antipa fidelissimo martyre interfecto in habitatione Satanae. Item ad Philadelphenorum, quod a tentatione ultima liberaretur, qui Domini nomen non negarat. Exinde victori cuique promittit nunc arborem vitae, et mortis veniam secundae: nunc latens manna cum calculo candido, et nomine ignoto: nunc ferreae virgae potestatem, et stellae matutinae claritatem: nunc albam vestiri, nec deleri de libro vitae, et columnam fieri in Dei templo, in nomine Dei et Domini, et Jerusalem coelestis inscripta, nunc residere cum Domino in throno ejus, quod aliquando Zebedaei filiis negabatur. Quinam isti tam beati victores, nisi proprie martyres? Illorum etenim victoriae, quorum et pugnae; eorum vero pugnae, quorum et sanguis. Sed et interim sub altari martyrum animae placidum quiescunt, et fiducia ultionis patientiam pascunt, et indutae stolis, candidam claritatis usurpant, donec et alii consortium illarum gloriae impleant. Nam et rursus innumera multitudo albati et palmis victoriae insignes revelantur; scilicet de Antichristo triumphantes, sicut unus ex presbyteris; Hi sunt, ait, qui veniunt ex illa pressura magna, et laverunt vestimentum suum, et candidaverunt ipsum in sanguine agni: vestitus enim animae, caro. Sordes quidem baptismate abluuntur, maculae vero martyrio candidantur. Quia et Esaias ex russeo et coccino niveum et laneum repromittit. Magna etiam Babylon cum describitur ebria sanctorum cruore, sine dubio ebrietas ejus martyriorum poculis ministratur, quorum formido quid relatura sit, aeque ostenditur. Inter omnes enim reprobos; imo ante omnes. Timidis autem, inquit, dehinc caeteris, particula in stagno ignis et sulphuris. Sic timor ejus in Epistola ejus, quem dilectio foras abjicit, habet poenam.
pass_a_gloss: Who now would know the innermost parts of the Scriptures more than the school of Christ itself? Whom the Lord also adopted as disciples for Himself, so that they might be taught all things; and He adorned them as teachers for us, so that they might teach all things. To whom would He rather have declared the figure of His voice, than to him to whom He revealed the image of His glory, to Peter, James, John, and afterwards to Paul, whom He also made a partaker of paradise before his martyrdom? Or do they also write otherwise than they think, as masters of deceit, not of truth? Peter indeed to the Pontics: For what glory is it, he says, if you are not punished as evildoers, but you endure? For this is grace, and for this you were called, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you might follow His footsteps. And again: Beloved, do not be terrified at the fiery trial which is being brought upon you to test you, as though something new were happening to you; but to the extent that you share in the sufferings of Christ, rejoice, so that you may also rejoice exulting in the revelation of His glory. If you are reviled in the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the glory and Spirit of God rest upon you, provided that none of you suffer as a murderer, or thief, or evildoer, or coveter of another's property. But if as a Christian, let him not be ashamed; but let him glorify the Lord in that name. John indeed exhorts us to lay down our lives for our brethren, denying that there is fear in love: For perfect love casts out fear; because fear has punishment; and he who fears is not perfect in love. What fear is it that is understood, except the fear of denial? What perfect love does he affirm, except the love that drives out fear and inspires confession? What punishment does fear inflict, except the punishment that the denier will suffer, to be killed in Gehenna, body and soul? And if one must die for one's brethren, how much more must one die for the Lord, as he teaches, sufficiently instructed also from his own Apocalypse! For the Spirit commanded the angel of the church of Smyrna: Behold, the devil will cast some of you into prison, that you may be tested for ten days. Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life. Likewise to the Pergamenes, concerning Antipas, the most faithful martyr, who was slain in the habitation of Satan. Likewise to the Philadelphians, that they might be freed from the final temptation, who did not deny the name of the Lord. From that time on, He promises to each conqueror now the tree of life, and exemption from the second death; now hidden manna with a white stone, and an unknown name; now the power of a rod of iron, and the brightness of the morning star; now to be clothed in white, and not to be blotted out of the book of life, and to become a pillar in the temple of God, in the name of God and the Lord, and the heavenly Jerusalem inscribed, now to sit with the Lord on His throne, which was once denied to the sons of Zebedee. Who are these most blessed conquerors, if not properly martyrs? For theirs are the victories, and theirs are the battles; and theirs is the blood. But also meanwhile, under the altar, the souls of the martyrs rest in peace, and with confidence of vengeance, they nourish patience, and clothed in white robes, they take on the brightness of clarity, until others also fulfill the fellowship of their glory. For also again, a countless multitude, clothed in white and marked with the palm of victory, are revealed; clearly, they are triumphing over the Antichrist, as one of the presbyters says: These are they who come from the great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb; for the garment of the soul is the flesh. The filth is indeed washed away by baptism, but the stains are made white by martyrdom. Because also Isaiah promises from the red and the scarlet, something white and woolly. Great Babylon is also described as drunk with the blood of the saints, without doubt, her drunkenness is served by the cups of the martyrs, whose fear will show what it will bring, equally. Among all the reprobates; indeed, before all. But to the timid, he says, henceforth, a part in the lake of fire and sulfur. Thus the fear of which love casts out has a punishment, as is shown in His Epistle.

pass_b_english: Who today knows the innermost depths of Scripture better than Christ's own school? The Lord adopted the apostles as his own disciples so they would be taught everything, and he appointed them as our teachers so they would teach everything. To whom would he have disclosed the sound of his voice rather than to those to whom he revealed the image of his glory — Peter, James, John, and later Paul, whom he made a partaker of paradise before his martyrdom? Or do they write something other than what they think, as masters of deceit instead of truth? Peter tells the Pontics: 'What glory is it if you are not punished as evildoers but endure?' (1 Peter 2:20). 'This is grace; for this you were called, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you might follow in his steps.' And again: 'Beloved, do not be terrified by the fiery ordeal taking place among you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you; but rejoice to the extent that you share in Christ's sufferings, so that you may also rejoice exulting when his glory is revealed' (1 Peter 3:14). 'If you are reviled in the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the glory and Spirit of God rest upon you — provided none of you suffers as a murderer, thief, evildoer, or meddler. But if as a Christian, let him not be ashamed; let him glorify the Lord in that name.' John exhorts us to lay down our lives for our brothers and sisters, denying that fear exists in love: 'Perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment; and whoever fears is not perfected in love' (1 John 4:18). What fear is understood except the fear of denial? What perfect love does he affirm except the love that drives out fear and inspires confession? What punishment does fear inflict except the punishment the denier will suffer — to be killed in Gehenna, body and soul? And if one must die for one's brothers, how much more must one die for the Lord, as he teaches, sufficiently instructed from his own Apocalypse! The Spirit commanded the angel of the church in Smyrna: 'Behold, the devil will throw some of you into prison so that you may be tested for ten days. Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life' (Revelation 2:10). Likewise to the Pergamenes concerning Antipas, the faithful martyr slain where Satan dwells. Likewise to the Philadelphians, that they would be kept from the final trial because they did not deny the Lord's name. From then on he promises each conqueror: the tree of life and exemption from the second death; hidden manna with a white stone and a new name; authority of an iron rod and the brightness of the morning star; to be clothed in white, never blotted from the book of life, and made a pillar in God's temple bearing the name of God and the Lord and the new Jerusalem; to sit with the Lord on his throne — a privilege once denied to the sons of Zebedee. Who are these supremely blessed conquerors if not the martyrs themselves? Theirs are the victories, theirs the battles, theirs the blood. Meanwhile, under the altar, the souls of the martyrs rest in peace; confident of vengeance, they feed their patience, and clothed in white robes they wear the brightness of purity until others complete the fellowship of their glory. Again, a countless multitude robed in white and bearing victory palms appears — those who have conquered the Antichrist, as one of the elders says: 'These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb' (Revelation 7:14). For the garment of the soul is the flesh. Filth is washed away by baptism, but stains are whitened by martyrdom. Isaiah promises that from crimson and scarlet shall come white as wool. Great Babylon is described as drunk on the blood of the saints; without doubt, her drunkenness is supplied by the cups of the martyrs, whose fear reveals what it will bring — equally. Among all the reprobates; indeed, before all of them. 'But to the timid,' he says, 'and the rest, a portion in the lake of fire and sulfur.' Thus the fear that love casts out carries its own punishment, as shown in his Epistle.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful literal gloss, and Pass B provides a fluent English version that correctly incorporates the required inline scripture citations (1 Peter 2:20, 1 Peter 3:14, 1 John 4:18, Revelation 2:10, Revelation 7:14) corresponding to the quoted/alluded Latin passages. All nuances regarding agency and doctrine are preserved.
